newsitem.title: CHILE: Codelco's El Teniente studies copper output hike.
newsitem.headline: Codelco's El Teniente studies copper output hike.

text.p: El Teniente division of Chile state copper company Codelco is studying plans to increase its copper production to 500,000 tonnes in 2000 from 350,000 tonnes currently, said the pit's strategic planning director Armando Olavarria.

"El Teniente has the reserves and now we are looking at the best way to extract them," Olavarria told Reuters by telephone from the mine. "We are analyzing alternatives for increasing production to 500,000 tonnes in 2000."
El Teniente, Codelco's second largest division, will decide by the end of the year on how to exploit its reserves to increase the pit's copper output, he said.
The mine hopes to maintain production at 500,000 tonnes for at least four or five years and is studing ways to keep it at this level for up to 15 years, he said.
"We are studying other projects to maintain production in the long term," said Olavarria.
The new production will not be phased in but will come on stream in a single jump, he said.
The mine, which lies in the Andes south of Santiago, has known reserves of two billion tonnes with routine exploration regularly uncovering new mineral ore bodies.

The expansion plans include extending El Teniente's large underground mine as well as building a small open-cast pit to exploit copper-rich mineral discarded on the surface as waste when the mine first started operating early this century.
Olavarria said the expansion will cost $500 million and be financed from Codelco's own resources.
The mine is already investing $160 million in the Esmeralda project which should start producing next year, making up for falling grades in the part of the pit known as level four.
El Teniente calculates that the new output will help the division cut cash costs to $0.38 a pound from $0.50 this year.

These low costs mean Codelco does not have to worry about finding buyers for the extra copper from El Teniente whose expansion plan comes just days after a major output hike announced by the huge Escondida pit.
"Our competitivity is in our costs. If we don't extract this mineral, then our competitors will," he said.
Olavarria said the division does expect production to be hurt by a drought in central Chile as the mine has taken measures to improve its water supplies.
Other mine officials have said the mine could face difficulties early next year as the result of the water shortage.
